amendments.rule:
Where English fuses several morphemes into one word, such as *wherein*, they share a unit. Reserve `added` for English that no morpheme licenses at all. This governs a fixed multi-word Hebrew expression the ASV renders with one English word too — `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles*, `אִם לֹא` → *surely*: the whole expression is one unit, headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme, rather than one rendered morpheme beside others marked `unrepresented`. The one-English-word condition is load-bearing in both directions: `בְּיַד` → *by* and `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* fuse, but where the ASV spends a second English word on the expression — `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses while the same idiom as *say ... nay* does not — the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. **Read that condition as one English rendering, not one English token.** A compound English preposition written in two or three words — *because of*, *by reason of*, *out of* — is a single rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and it fuses; so does an expression whose unit additionally carries a copula or other word the construction hands to the whole of it under another rule, as `לִפְנֵי` → *was before*. What defeats the condition is English the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so that each morpheme has a rendering of its own: `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives *to* to the preposition and *meet* to `פָּנֶה`, and `עַד לְ` → *until there was* gives *until* to `עַד` and the predicate's supplied copula to the `לְ` under rule 49, while the same `עַד לְ` → *to* fuses. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the second English word and ask whether a particular morpheme has lost its rendering or only the expression as a whole is diminished. What the second morpheme is tagged does not matter; a preposition before a construct noun fuses on the same terms as a compound preposition. Contiguity is part of the condition for such an expression: a verb and the preposition it governs, held apart by the subject or the object, is not one. It is not a condition on fusion generally — rule 35's *Nor* and *never* fuse across intervening material, because there the one English word still carries every morpheme's sense. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* and `הוֹסִיף ... אֶל` → *exceed* are a verb whose preposition the ASV's comparative recasting leaves unrendered, so rule 2 splits them and the preposition is `unrepresented`. Rule 22 governs a repetition of the *same* element, not the parts of an idiom.

**The expression need not be an idiom, and a full lexical noun fuses on the same terms as a function morpheme.** Where Hebrew writes a generic head noun before an attributive that names the class — `אִשָּׁה` or `אִישׁ` before a participle or an adjective — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme: `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* is one unit headed on `זוֹנָה`, with the indefinite article going to that nominal expression under rule 15, and `אִשָּׁה` is not marked `unrepresented` beside it. The one-English-word condition and its subtraction test decide this exactly as they decide a compound preposition — dropping the English word diminishes only the expression as a whole, and no morpheme owns a part of it — so where the ASV instead spends a word on each, as `אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה` → *man of war*, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. Do not read *fixed multi-word Hebrew expression* above as a requirement that the pair be idiomatic.

**For this rule, a particle's single idiomatic English rendering includes the pronouns the English formula requires.** The entreaty particle `נָא` → *I beseech thee* or *we pray thee* takes the complete formula, headed on *beseech* or *pray*; its English subject and object pronouns are not `added`, because they realize the particle's one entreaty rather than supply arguments of the neighbouring imperative. Where the ASV's formula omits an object, as *I pray*, align only what it writes.
amendments.why: JER.3 fused two morphemes onto one English word four times under this rule (3.1 מֵאִתּוֹ -> 'from', 3.6 אֶל־תַּחַת -> 'under', 3.10 בְּשֶׁקֶר -> 'feignedly', 3.11 נַפְשָׁהּ -> 'herself') and split the same shape at 3.3, marking אִשָּׁה unrepresented beside זוֹנָה -> 'harlot's'. What licensed the inconsistency was the opening clause's wording 'a fixed multi-word Hebrew expression', which a verse pass can read as excluding an ordinary noun-plus-attributive pair even though the rule's later sentence already says that what the second morpheme is tagged does not matter. The amendment closes that reading and nothing else: every existing clause, example and qualification is preserved verbatim, including the contiguity condition, the subtraction test, the compound-preposition and copula riders, the גָּדַל ... מִן exclusion, the rule 22 boundary and the נָא paragraph. Corpus support is the two units where a generic person-noun fuses into a single English word rather than going unrepresented, ISA.34.16 אִשָּׁה+לֹא and EXO.12.22 לֹא+אִישׁ, both noncompositional 'none'; the targeted query LEMMA=אִשָּׁה NEXT=Vqrfsa returned nothing, so no corpus unit contradicts the amendment and none states it either. The added אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה -> 'man of war' counterexample keeps the one-English-word condition doing the limiting work, so the amendment cannot be read as licensing fusion whenever a generic noun stands beside an attributive.

conventions: Interrogative he: all five occurrences in this chapter (3.1 twice, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6) are marked unrepresented. The ASV signals each question by subject-auxiliary inversion, and the fronted auxiliary (Will, Wilt, Hast) belongs to the imperfect or perfect verb under rule 17. The corpus is genuinely divided here — 140 units unrepresented against roughly 96 aligned to the fronted auxiliary, with most of the aligned ones conceding the unrepresented reading in their notes — so this is a chapter-wide choice rather than a settled ruling, and it is the reason for the Ti BSB disagreements.

Rule 30 fusion is applied throughout this chapter wherever the ASV renders two source morphemes by a single English word, and the unit heads on the morpheme carrying the lexeme except where both are function words: מֵאִתּוֹ -> 'from' (3.1, headed on מִן as first token, both morphemes being prepositions), אֶל־תַּחַת -> 'under' (3.6, on תַּחַת), בְּשֶׁקֶר -> 'feignedly' (3.10, on שֶׁקֶר), נַפְשָׁהּ -> 'herself' (3.11, on נֶפֶשׁ), and אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה -> 'harlot's' (3.3, on זוֹנָה, corrected at reconciliation). The last of these establishes that a full lexical noun fuses on the same terms as a preposition or a suffix; do not mark one of the pair unrepresented to avoid a noncompositional unit.

שְׁפִי is rendered 'bare heights' at 3.2 and 3.21 and both units are headed on 'bare', by rule 31's subtraction: 'heights' alone is any heights, while שְׁפִי names the barren height, exactly as בָּמָה -> 'high place' heads on 'high'. The competing reading, heading on 'heights' as the English phrase's noun, is recorded in both units' notes.

report: Checked all 63 candidate lemma groups plus the full dump end to end. One genuine cross-verse split found: rule 30 fusion. The chapter fuses two source morphemes onto one English word four times (JER.3.1 מֵאִתּוֹ -> 'from'; JER.3.6 אֶל־תַּחַת -> 'under'; JER.3.10 בְּשֶׁקֶר -> 'feignedly'; JER.3.11 נַפְשָׁהּ -> 'herself') and does the opposite at JER.3.3, marking אִשָּׁה unrepresented beside זוֹנָה -> 'harlot's'. Rule 30 rules against that shape in terms ('rather than one rendered morpheme beside others marked unrepresented'; 'what the second morpheme is tagged does not matter'). JER.3.3 patched to a noncompositional unit on s010+s011, headed on זוֹנָה / 'harlot's'.

Evidence round outcome. (1) LEMMA=אִשָּׁה NEXT=Vqrfsa returned nothing, so JER.3.3 was decided from the contract and the chapter's own four-fold practice, not from precedent; the nearest corpus support is ISA.34.16 אִשָּׁה+לֹא and EXO.12.22 לֹא+אִישׁ, both noncompositional 'none', where a generic person-noun fuses rather than going unrepresented. (2) The interrogative particle comes back 140 unrepresented against roughly 96 aligned to a fronted auxiliary, and most of the aligned units carry [medium] notes conceding the unrepresented reading; JER.3's five unrepresented Ti tokens are consistent and are the plurality reading. (3) LEMMA=וְ TARGET='^who$' returned 5/5 aligned, confirming JER.3.15's waw -> 'who'; rule 17's caution does not bite, because no explicit subject pronoun stands in that clause.

BSB disagreements are convention differences, not errors. R x 11 are rule 40 recastings where the ASV spends no word on what the preposition contributes (שָׁמַע בְּקוֹל -> 'obeyed the voice' at 3.13 and 3.25; קָרָא לְ -> 'call me' at 3.19; dative לְ -> bare indirect object at 3.15 and 3.19). Td x 13 are articles left unrepresented where a demonstrative supplies the phrase's single determiner, which rule 29 settles with its own הֶעָרִים הָאֵלֶּה -> 'these cities'. Ti x 5 is the particle above. The three אֵת tokens are rule 16's majority ruling; JER.3.8 הָ has no possessive written ('a bill of divorcement'); JER.3.12 Sh is rule 32 and JER.3.12 י is silenced by the 'look in anger' recasting. JER.3.3 אִשָּׁה now reads as represented, but as a consequence of the rule 30 correction, not to move the rate.

Not splits, checked and left. The הַ groups divide on whether a demonstrative licenses the determiner; the בְּ and לְ groups on rule 40; the אֵת groups on rule 16's three families; supplied 'it' is added at 3.5, 3.7 and 3.16 and aligned at 3.16 exactly where a suffix is present, which is rule 44 applied uniformly. JER.3.20's added 'as' stands: rule 55 is literal about a protasis writing no conjunction, כֵּן sits in the apodosis and takes 'so', and the verse pass named the correlative-pair reading in its note. JER.3.8's כָּל -> 'very' and JER.3.11's 'more ... than' on מִן are single occurrences with their competing readings recorded, so there is nothing to reconcile them against.

One amendment proposed, to rule 30 rather than as a new rule: the phrase 'fixed multi-word Hebrew expression' is what let JER.3.3 read a generic head noun plus its classifying attributive as falling outside the fusion condition. The amendment says the expression need not be an idiom, adds אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה -> 'man of war' as the limiting counterexample, and leaves every existing clause of rule 30 intact.
